There is a SmallRye GraphQL card for our application. The GraphQL Schema is the generated schema definition. And the GraphQL UI is the an interactive UI for developers to test the GraphQL operations directly.

Click the GraphQL UI to open the Graph UI page.

Try to perform an allPosts query and click the execute button, you will will the following page.

To get a post by ID, try the following query instead, it requires an extra argument. Set the postId variable in the Query variables input box, it is JSON format.

If the postId is a non-existing id, it will return a null result like this.

{
    "data":{
        "postById":null
    }
}

You can define a custom Exception and convert it into a GraphQL error.

docs.title: Exception Handling
docs.text:
Create a PostNotFoundException.

import io.smallrye.graphql.api.ErrorCode;

@ErrorCode("POST_NOT_FOUND")
public class PostNotFoundException extends RuntimeException{

    public PostNotFoundException(String id) {
        super("Post: "+ id +" was not found.");
    }
}

And add the following configuration in the application.properties.

mp.graphql.showErrorMessage=com.example.demo.PostNotFoundException
smallrye.graphql.errorExtensionFields=exception,classification,code,description,validationErrorType,queryPath

Run the application again, and provide a non-existing post ID, then execute the query. As you see the errors is added into the query result, it includes the code and message you have defined in your exception class.

docs.title: Resolving Fields
docs.text:
In our former example, a Post includes the comments fields directly, it is an eager approach. In a real world application, you could want to fetch data of the related comments on demand. When a comments field is set in the result field list of a query string, it could hit the backend database or retrieve from cache and return the result for the specified post ID.

@GraphQLApi
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class GraphQLResource {
    final PostService postService;

    public int comments(@Source Post post) {
        return postService.commentsByPostId(post.getId());
    }
}

You can also apply the resolving rule on some virtual fields( here I mean those are not existed in the backend database and evaluated at runtime), there are some examples :

// calculate the comments count of a specified post
public int countOfComments(@Source Post post) {
     return ...
}

// retrieve the current user info from the GraphQL context 
// and determine if he/her has voted the current post
public boolean voted(@Source Post post, @Context context) {
     return ...
}

docs.title: Input Validation
docs.text:
You can apply some bean validation annotations on the input type to check if it satisfies your requirements.

public class CreatePost {

    @NotEmpty//add hibernate-validator, else bean validation dose not work.
    @Length(min = 5)
    String title;

    String content;
}

And do not forget to add the hibernate-validator extension into the project deps.

mvn quarkus:add-extension -Dextensions="hibernate-validator"

Run the application and have a try. Leave the title empty , hit the execute button, the validation exceptions are converted into GraphQL errors.

In this post, we have not explored the Subscription type - the messaging contract in the GraphQL specification. We will discuss it in the further posts.

docs.title: Building Reactive APIs with Quarkus
docs.text:
As you know, Quarkus has built-in Jaxrs support with RESTEasy when you are creating a Quarkus application.

Most of developers are familiar with the imperative programming methods like this.

@GET
@Produces(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
public String hello() {
    return "hello";
}

In Quarkus, you can use ReactiveStreams Publisher as return type.

@GET
@Produces(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
public Publisher<String> hello() {
    return "hello";
}

Besides the standard ReactiveStreams APIs, you can also use Java 8 CompletableFuture, RxJava 2, and SmallRye Munity.

For the database connecting to the underlay database, you can switch to the Reactive PostgresSQL Client or Reactive MySQL Client.

Currently Hibernate core and JPA do not support ReactiveStreams APIs, but there is a new sub project under Hibernate which is trying to do this problem, see Hibernate RX.

In this post, we will refactor the sample used in the former post, and reimplement it by using the reactive features in Quarkus.

We will start with SmallRye Munity which may be new to developers including me, and then we will explore the Java 8 CompletableFuture and RxJava 2.

First of all, create a Quarkus project quickly using Quarkus coding if you want to work on a new project, and add Resteasy Munity, Reactive Pg Client to dependencies.

Or running the following command to add required Quarkus extensions to the existing Quarkus project. 

mvn quarkus:add-extension -Dextension=resteasy-mutiny 
mvn quarkus:add-extension -Dextension=reactive-pg-client

SmallRye Munity implements the ReactiveStreams specification, and provides two conventional classes - Uni and Multi.

  • Uni - handle stream of 0..1 items
  • Multi - handle stream of 0..n items (potentially unbounded)

The Reactive Pg Client is derived from Vertx Reactive Pg Client, with the help of Quarkus, you can configure database connection in the application.properties directly, and inject the reactive Postgres Client PgPool bean in your codes.

Let's have a look at the Post class, there is no extra annotations on this version.

public class Post {
    UUID id;
    String title;
    String content;
    LocalDateTime createdAt;
    // ...
}

And move to the Repository class, which is use for performing CRUD operations on table posts.

@ApplicationScoped
public class PostRepository {
    private static final Logger LOGGER = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PostRepository.class);

    private final PgPool client;

    @Inject
    public PostRepository(PgPool _client) {
        this.client = _client;
    }

    public Uni<List<Post>> findAll() {
        return this.client
                .query("SELECT * FROM posts")
                .map(rs -> {
                    var result = new ArrayList<Post>(rs.size());
                    for (Row row : rs) {
                        result.add(this.rowToPost(row));
                    }
                    return result;
                });
    }

    public Uni<Post> findById(UUID id) {
        return this.client
                .preparedQuery("SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id=$1", Tuple.of(id))
                .map(RowSet::iterator)
                .map(it -> it.hasNext() ? rowToPost(it.next()) :null);
               // .flatMap(it -> it.hasNext() ? Uni.createFrom().item(rowToPost(it.next())) : Uni.createFrom().failure(()-> new PostNotFoundException()));
    }

    private Post rowToPost(Row row) {
        return Post.of(row.getUUID("id"), row.getString("title"), row.getString("content"), row.getLocalDateTime("created_at"));
    }

    public Uni<UUID> save(Post data) {
        return this.client
                .preparedQuery("INSERT INTO posts (title, content) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING (id)", Tuple.of(data.getTitle(), data.getContent()))
                .map(RowSet::iterator)
                .map(it -> it.hasNext() ? it.next().getUUID("id") : null);
    }

    public Uni<Integer> update(UUID id, Post data) {
        return this.client
                .preparedQuery("UPDATE posts SET title=$1, content=$2 WHERE id=$3", Tuple.of(data.getTitle(), data.getContent(), id))
                .map(RowSet::rowCount);
    }

    public Uni<Integer> deleteAll() {
        return client.query("DELETE FROM posts")
                .map(RowSet::rowCount);
    }

    public Uni<Integer> delete(UUID id) {
        return client.preparedQuery("DELETE FROM posts WHERE id=$1", Tuple.of(id))
                .map(RowSet::rowCount);
    }

}

In the above codes,

The PgPool is imported from package io.vertx.mutiny.pgclient, there are several variants for different underlay implementations.

The preparedQuaery method accepts a second parameter and bind them to the SQL statements.

The RowSet::rowCount return the number of the affected rows when performing a update or deletion queries.

In the findAll and find methods, use map to transform a RowSet to our custom Post instance.

Now let's explore the changes in PostResource.

@Path("/posts")
@RequestScoped
public class PostResource {
    private final static Logger LOGGER = Logger.getLogger(PostResource.class.getName());

    private final PostRepository posts;

    @Inject
    public PostResource(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GET
    @Produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    public Uni<Response> getAllPosts() {
        return this.posts.findAll().map(data -> ok(data).build());
    }

    @POST
    @Consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    public Uni<Response> savePost(@Valid Post post) {
        return this.posts.save(post)
                .map(id -> created(URI.create("/posts/" + id)).build());
    }

    @Path("{id}")
    @GET
    @Produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    public Uni<Response> getPostById(@PathParam("id") final String id) {
        return this.posts.findById(UUID.fromString(id))
                .map(data -> {
                    if (data == null) {
                        return null;
                    }
                    return ok(data).build();
                })
                .onItem().ifNull().continueWith(status(Status.NOT_FOUND).build());
        //.onFailure(PostNotFoundException.class).recoverWithItem(status(Status.NOT_FOUND).build());
    }

    @Path("{id}")
    @PUT
    @Consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    public Uni<Response> updatePost(@PathParam("id") final String id, @Valid Post post) {
        return this.posts.update(UUID.fromString(id), post)
                .map(updated -> updated > 0 ? Status.NO_CONTENT : Status.NOT_FOUND)
                .map(status -> status(status).build());
    }

    @DELETE
    @Path("{id}")
    public Uni<Response> delete(@PathParam("id") String id) {
        return this.posts.delete(UUID.fromString(id))
                .map(deleted -> deleted > 0 ? Status.NO_CONTENT : Status.NOT_FOUND)
                .map(status -> status(status).build());
    }
}

Yes, with the help of resteasy-munity extension, you can return Uni or Multi types in the Jaxrs resources.

Let's take a closer look at the getPostById method in the above PostResource, it looks a little ugly. In our PostRepository class, the findById return a Uni, when there is a Post found return back a Uni<Post>, else there is a null in the Uni stream. So in getPostById we have to filter out it in the main flow and handle the null case in the onItem().ifNull(). For my opinion, it is a little tedious, currently there is no replacement of switchIfEmpty like methods in Munity.

To make it more understandable, use a custom exception in PostRepository like this.

public Uni<Post> findById(UUID id) {
    return this.client
        .preparedQuery("SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id=$1", Tuple.of(id))
        .map(RowSet::iterator)
        .flatMap(it -> it.hasNext() ? Uni.createFrom().item(rowToPost(it.next())) : Uni.createFrom().failure(()-> new PostNotFoundException()));
}

And in the PostResource class, handle this exception in the onFailter event.

@Path("{id}")
@GET
@Produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
public Uni<Response> getPostById(@PathParam("id") final String id) {
    return this.posts.findById(UUID.fromString(id))
        .map(data -> ok(data).build())
        .onFailure(PostNotFoundException.class).recoverWithItem(status(Status.NOT_FOUND).build());
}

In the application.properties file, configure the datasource like this.

quarkus.datasource.url = vertx-reactive:postgresql://localhost:5432/blogdb
quarkus.datasource.username = user
quarkus.datasource.password = password

Similar with the Jdbc datasource, but here it use the prefix vertx-reactive: in the connection url.

Like the former post, we will use a DataInitializer bean to insert some sample data at the application startup.

@ApplicationScoped
public class DataInitializer {
    private final static Logger LOGGER = Logger.getLogger(DataInitializer.class.getName());

    @Inject
    PgPool client;

    public void onStart(@Observes StartupEvent ev) {
        LOGGER.info("The application is starting...");

        Tuple first = Tuple.of("Hello Quarkus", "My first post of Quarkus");
        Tuple second = Tuple.of("Hello Again, Quarkus", "My second post of Quarkus");

        client.query("DELETE FROM posts")
                .flatMap(result -> client.preparedBatch("INSERT INTO posts (title, content) VALUES ($1, $2)", List.of(first, second)))
                .flatMap(rs -> client.query("SELECT * FROM posts"))
                .subscribe()
                .with(
                        rows -> rows.forEach(r -> System.out.println(r)),
                        err -> System.out.println(err)
                );

    }
}

As mentioned, in a Quarkus application, you can also use Java 8 CompletableFuture or RxJava 2 APIs if you prefer them.

Let's have a look the version of using Java 8 CompletableFuture.

The Repository class.

@ApplicationScoped
public class PostRepository {
    private static final Logger LOGGER = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PostRepository.class);

    private final PgPool client;

    @Inject
    public PostRepository(PgPool _client) {
        this.client = _client;
    }

    public CompletionStage<List<Post>> findAll() {
        return client.query("SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY id ASC")
                .thenApply(rs -> StreamSupport.stream(rs.spliterator(), false)
                        .map(this::from)
                        .collect(Collectors.toList())
                );
    }

    private Post from(Row row) {
        return Post.of(row.getUUID("id"), row.getString("title"), row.getString("content"), row.getLocalDateTime("created_at"));
    }

    public CompletionStage<Post> findById(UUID id) {
        return client.preparedQuery("SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id=$1", Tuple.of(id))
                .thenApply(RowSet::iterator)
                .thenApply(iterator -> iterator.hasNext() ? from(iterator.next()) : null)
                .thenApply(Optional::ofNullable)
                .thenApply(p -> p.orElseThrow(() -> new PostNotFoundException(id)));
    }

    public CompletionStage<UUID> save(Post data) {
        return client.preparedQuery("INSERT INTO posts(title, content) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING (id)", Tuple.of(data.getTitle(), data.getContent()))
                .thenApply(rs -> rs.iterator().next().getUUID("id"));
    }

    public CompletionStage<Integer> update(UUID id, Post data) {

@ApplicationScoped
public class PostRepository {
    private static final Logger LOGGER = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PostRepository.class);

    private final PgPool client;

    @Inject
    public PostRepository(PgPool _client) {
        this.client = _client;
    }

    public Flowable<Post> findAll() {
        return this.client
                .rxBegin()
                .flatMapPublisher(
                        tx -> tx.rxPrepare("SELECT * FROM posts")
                                .flatMapPublisher(
                                        preparedQuery -> preparedQuery.createStream(50, Tuple.tuple())
                                                .toFlowable()
                                )
                                .doAfterTerminate(tx::rxCommit)

                )
                .map(this::rowToPost);
    }

    public Maybe<Post> findById(UUID id) {
        return this.client
                .rxPreparedQuery("SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id=$1", Tuple.of(id))
                .map(RowSet::iterator)
                .flatMapMaybe(it -> it.hasNext() ? Maybe.just(rowToPost(it.next())): Maybe.empty());
    }

    private Post rowToPost(Row row) {
        return Post.of(row.getUUID("id"), row.getString("title"), row.getString("content"), row.getLocalDateTime("created_at"));
    }

    public Single<UUID> save(Post data) {
        return this.client
                .rxBegin()
                .flatMap(
                        tx -> tx.rxPreparedQuery("INSERT INTO posts (title, content) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING (id)", Tuple.of(data.getTitle(), data.getContent()))
                                .toFlowable().firstOrError()
                                .doAfterTerminate(tx::rxCommit)
                )
                .map(RowSet::iterator)
                .map(it -> it.hasNext() ? it.next().getUUID("id") : null);
    }

    public Single<Integer> update(UUID id, Post data) {
        return this.client
                .rxPreparedQuery("UPDATE posts SET title=$1, content=$2 WHERE id=$3", Tuple.of(data.getTitle(), data.getContent(), id))
                .map(RowSet::rowCount);
    }

    public Single<Integer> deleteAll() {

                .map(RowSet::rowCount);
    }

        return client.rxPreparedQuery("DELETE FROM posts WHERE id=$1", Tuple.of(id))
                .map(RowSet::rowCount);
    }

docs.title: Interacting with REST APIs in Quarkus
docs.text:
In the last post, we used Spring compatible APIs to rebuild our original REST APIs in a Quarkus application. In this post, we will interact with the REST APIs in the client side.

There a few HTTP Client libraries used to communicate with REST APIs, such as Apache HTTPClient, OkHttp, etc. And Spring has specific RestTemplate, WebClient API can be used to interact with REST APIs. And Java 11 also ship a new stable HttpClient API.

Quarkus has built-in support of the latest Microprofile, which includes a Rest Client spec for this purpose, the Quarkus rest-client supports both MP RestClient and JAX-RS Client API. In this posts, we will explore MP RestClient, JAX-RS Client and Java 11 HttpClient one by one.

docs.title: MicroProfile Rest Client
docs.text:
First of all, let's have a look at how to use MP RestClient to consume REST APIs.

Generate a simple Quarkus application using Quarkus Coding, remember adding Rest Client into dependencies.

Create a simple interface PostResourceClient.

@Path("/posts")
@RegisterRestClient
public interface PostResourceClient {

    @Path("count")
    @GET
    @Produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    CompletionStage<Long> countAllPosts(@QueryParam("q") String q);

    @GET
    @Produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    CompletionStage<List<Post>> getAllPosts(
            @QueryParam("q") String q,
            @QueryParam("offset") @DefaultValue("0") int offset,
            @QueryParam("limit") @DefaultValue("10") int limit
    );
}

The class and method signature is similar with PostResource we have created in the former posts.

  • We declare an interface instead of a class.
  • The interface is annotated with the @RegisterRestClient annotation.
  • The method can return entity type directly or a Jaxrs's Response or Java 8's CompletionStage wrapper.

You can configure the baseUri in the application.properties, or set baseUri attribute the @RegisterRestClient annotation.

Here is an example of the configuration in the application.properties.

com.example.PostResourceClient/mp-rest/url=http://localhost:8080
com.example.PostResourceClient/mp-rest/scope=javax.inject.Singleton

By default it uses the full qualified name of the Rest Client class as prefix of the config key. To change this, just set configKey attribute in the @RegisterRestClient annotation.

To use the PostResourceClient in your CDI bean, just inject it by @Inject with a CDI qualifier @RestClient.

@Path("/api")
@RequestScoped
public class PostController {
    @Inject
    @RestClient
    PostResourceClient client;

    @GET
    @Produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    public CompletionStage<PostPage> getAllPosts(
            @QueryParam("q") String q,
            @QueryParam("offset") @DefaultValue("0") int offset,
            @QueryParam("limit") @DefaultValue("10") int limit
    ) {
        return this.client.getAllPosts(q, offset, limit)
                .thenCombine(
                        this.client.countAllPosts(q),
                        (data, count) -> PostPage.of(data, count)
                );
    }

}

The above getAllPosts method is trying to combine the data and count into a new PostPage instance.

To test if the client is working as expected. Firstly you should start the server side application to serve the REST APIs. Run it by mvn quarkus:dev command.

Then run the client application we are building by mvn quarkus:dev again.

$ curl http://localhost:8081/api/
{"content":[{"content":"My second post of Quarkus","createdAt":"2020-04-02T17:02:06.453988","id":"768a980f-b617-40c1-ba07-60759045d6b7","title":"Hello Again, Quarkus"},{"content":"My first post of Quarkus","createdAt":"2020-04-02T17:02:06.452993","id":"675bf657-fce4-4724-96c3-a2e2bf38ad58","title":"Hello Quarkus"}],"count":2}

In our PostResource , to access a none existing post resource, it will return a 404 HTTP status. Add the following method signature in the PostResouceClient.

public interface PostResourceClient {
    ...
    @GET
    @Path("{id}")
    @Produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    CompletionStage<Post> getPostById(@PathParam("id") String id);
}

And create a new method in the PostController to invoke the above APIs.

public class PostController {
    ...
    @GET
    @Path("{id}")
    @Produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    public CompletionStage<Post> getPost(@PathParam("id") String id ){
        return this.client.getPostById(id);
    }
}

When accessing a none existing post in the client application, it also return a 404 HTTP status.

If you do not want MP Rest Client to convert it automatically, you can use ResponseExceptionMapper to convert the failure status into a custom exception, and that leave room for you to handle it as you expected.

public class PostResponseExceptionMapper implements ResponseExceptionMapper<RuntimeException> {
    @Override
    public RuntimeException toThrowable(Response response) {
        if(response.getStatus()==404) {
            return  new PostNotFoundException("post not found, original cause:" + response.readEntity(String.class));
        }

        return null;
    }
}

And register it on the PostResourceClient class with a @RegisterProvider annotation.

@RegisterProvider(PostResponseExceptionMapper.class)
public interface PostResourceClient {}

Now, trying to accessing a none existing post resource, it will throw an PostNotFoundException in the background.

As an example, you can handle this exception with a custom ExceptionMapper in our client application. Check the PostNotFoundExceptionMapper yourself.

docs.title: JAX-RS Client API
docs.text:
Besides the declarative means provided in MP Rest Client, JAX-RS 2.0 provides a Client API to shake hands with the REST APIs in a programmatic way.

Let's have a look at the JAX-RS version of PostResourceClient.

@ApplicationScoped
public class PostResourceClient {
    private ExecutorService executorService = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();
    private Client client;
    private String baseUrl ;//= "http://localhost:8080";

    @Inject
    public PostResourceClient(PostServiceProperties properties) {
        baseUrl = properties.getBaseUrl();
        client = ClientBuilder.newBuilder()
                .executorService(executorService)
                .build();
    }

    CompletionStage<Long> countAllPosts(String q) {
        return client.target(baseUrl + "/posts/count")
                .queryParam("q", q)
                .request()
                .rx()
                .get(Long.class);
    }

    CompletionStage<List<Post>> getAllPosts(
            String q,
            int offset,
            int limit
    ) {
        return client.target(baseUrl + "/posts")
                .queryParam("q", q)
                .queryParam("offset", offset)
                .queryParam("limit", limit)
                .request()
                .rx()
                .get(new GenericType<List<Post>>() {});
    }

}

It uses the JAX-RS's ClientBuilder to build a Client firstly, then use it to call REST APIs.

The PostServiceProperties is a MP config class to read external configuration from the application.properties file.

@ConfigProperties(prefix = "post-service")
public class PostServiceProperties {
    private String baseUrl;

    public String getBaseUrl() {
        return baseUrl;
    }

    public void setBaseUrl(String baseUrl) {
        this.baseUrl = baseUrl;
    }
}

And the content of the application.properties file.

post-service.base-url=http://localhost:8080

But if you are using the JAX-RS client API, you should handle exceptions manually. For example, calling the REST API like this in the PostResourceClient.

Post getPostById(String id) {
    try (Response getPostByIdResponse = client.target(baseUrl + "/posts/" + id)
         .request().get()) {
        if (getPostByIdResponse.getStatus() == 404) {
            throw new PostNotFoundException(id);
        }

        return getPostByIdResponse.readEntity(Post.class);
    }

}

Next, let's look at the HttpClient in Java 11.

docs.title: Java 11 HttpClient
docs.text:
If you are using Java 11, it is luckily to use the brand new HttpClient API which is stabilized to public since Java 11.

The following is a new version using Java 11 HttpClient.

@ApplicationScoped
public class PostResourceClient {

    private final ExecutorService executorService = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5);

    private final HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.newBuilder()
            .executor(executorService)
            .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)
            .build();


    public PostResourceClient() {
    }

    CompletionStage<Long> countAllPosts(String q) {
       return  this.httpClient
                .sendAsync(
                        HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                                .GET()
                                .uri(URI.create("http://localhost:8080/posts/count?q=" + q))
                                .header("Accept", "application/json")
                                .build()
                        ,
                        HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
                )
                .thenApply(HttpResponse::body)
                .thenApply(Long::parseLong)
                .toCompletableFuture();

    }

    CompletionStage<List<Post>> getAllPosts(
            String q,
            int offset,
            int limit
    ) {
        return  this.httpClient
                .sendAsync(
                        HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                                .GET()
                                .uri(URI.create("http://localhost:8080/posts?q=" + q + "&offset=" + offset + "&limit=" + limit))
                                .header("Accept", "application/json")
                                .build()
                        ,
                        HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
                )
                .thenApply(HttpResponse::body)
                .thenApply(stringHttpResponse -> JsonbBuilder.newBuilder().build().fromJson(stringHttpResponse, new TypeLiteral<List<Post>>() {}.getType()))
                .thenApply(data ->(List<Post>)data)
                .toCompletableFuture();
    }

}

In the getAllPosts method , it uses JSON-B to convert the raw HTTP messages from String to a List<Post>.

docs.text:
You need Java 25 and a container runtime if you want Quarkus Dev Services to start PostgreSQL. The module sets maven.compiler.release to 25 and uses Quarkus 4.0.0.CR1.

The active datasource configuration sets the database kind to PostgreSQL but does not set a connection URL. Use Dev Services with a container runtime or configure a PostgreSQL connection. Hibernate schema generation is drop-and-create; use a disposable database.

docs.title: Follow the API structure
docs.text:
The Post entity maps a post to the database. The CreatePostRequest record validates incoming JSON: title cannot be blank and is limited to 100 characters; content cannot be blank.

The PostRepository uses PanacheRepositoryBase<Post, UUID> and returns Mutiny Uni and Multi values. The PostResources class maps the /posts resource to repository operations.

The create handler validates the request, persists a post, and returns a 201 Created response with a Location header:

@POST
@Consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
public Uni<Response> savePost(@Valid CreatePostRequest formData) {
    var post = Post.builder()
            .title(formData.title())
            .content(formData.content())
            .build();
    return this.posts.persist(post)
            .map(saved -> created(URI.create("/posts/" + saved.id)).build());
}

The resource also exposes GET /posts, GET /posts/{id}, PUT /posts/{id}, and DELETE /posts/{id}.

docs.title: Inspect the Spring API
docs.text:
The PostController uses Spring MVC annotations for /posts. GET /posts accepts page and size and returns a Spring Data Page<Post>. GET /posts/{id} reads a post; the create, update, and delete handlers write posts.

The PostRepository extends Spring Data JpaRepository. Its custom interface and implementation provide keyword search: GET /posts/search?q=... filters post title and content using a JPA Criteria query and supports offset/limit pagination. The module's POM includes the Quarkus Spring Web, Spring DI, Spring Data JPA, and PostgreSQL extensions.

PostExceptionHandler shows the sample's exception handling approaches. It maps a missing post to a structured 404 response and demonstrates @ExceptionHandler methods with ResponseEntity, @ResponseStatus, and the servlet response API.

The create handler accepts a validated request object and returns a 201 Created response with a Location header:

@PostMapping()
public ResponseEntity<Void> createPost(
        @RequestBody @Valid CreatePostCommand post) {
    Post data = Post.of(post.getTitle(), post.getContent());
    Post saved = this.postRepository.save(data);

    return created(
            ResteasyUriBuilder.fromTemplate("/posts/{id}")
                    .build(saved.getId())
                    .normalize()
    ).build();
}

docs.title: Hibernate Reactive with Panache
docs.text: Use the rest sample to build Quarkus REST endpoints on Hibernate Reactive with Panache. This module combines a Panache repository, Mutiny types, and a reactive PostgreSQL client.

docs.title: Sample structure
docs.text:
The module's POM includes quarkus-hibernate-reactive, quarkus-reactive-pg-client, and quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache. PostRepository implements PanacheRepositoryBase<Post, UUID>. Its query methods return Mutiny Uni values, and PostResources maps them to HTTP responses.

The active datasource kind is PostgreSQL. The sample does not set a URL; configure one or let Dev Services start a database. Hibernate schema generation uses drop-and-create, so use a disposable database.

docs.title: Run the sample
docs.text:
From the rest directory, run:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev. The API uses /posts. The getting-started recipe shows a create request and test command.

The resource exposes the posts API with Mutiny Uni values. Check the module's application.properties and Dev Services settings before starting PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Customize Jackson
docs.text: The rest module uses Jackson with Quarkus REST and customizes its JsonMapper through a CDI bean. The multipart module also customizes Jackson, with additional empty-value inclusion settings.

docs.title: Customize date and time output
docs.text:
The rest/CustomObjectMapper implements JsonMapperBuilderCustomizer. It disables date and time timestamp features:

@ApplicationScoped
public class CustomObjectMapper implements JsonMapperBuilderCustomizer {

    @Override
    public void customize(JsonMapper.Builder builder) {
        builder.disable(DateTimeFeature.WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS);
        builder.disable(DateTimeFeature.WRITE_DATE_TIMESTAMPS_AS_NANOSECONDS);
        builder.disable(DateTimeFeature.READ_DATE_TIMESTAMPS_AS_NANOSECONDS);
    }
}

The rest POM includes quarkus-rest-jackson. Check that the selected customizer and the JSON extension match the REST stack used by your module.

docs.title: Compare the multipart Jackson settings
docs.text: The multipart/ObjectMapperConfig also disables date timestamps and changes default property inclusion to NON_EMPTY for values and contents. See Receive and send multipart data for the endpoints that use that configuration.

docs.title: Customize JSON-B
docs.text: The rest-classic sample uses JSON-B with RESTEasy Classic and customizes serialization through a CDI bean. Use this recipe to locate that customization; check the module's dependency versions before adapting it.

docs.title: Configure JSON-B
docs.text:
The module includes quarkus-resteasy-jsonb. Its CustomJsonbConfig implements JsonbConfigCustomizer. The customizer enables formatted output, omits null values, sets UTF-8 encoding, and installs a property visibility strategy that exposes fields rather than methods. This supports record serialization in the sample.

The rest-pgclient module also uses JSON-B through quarkus-rest-jsonb, but does not add the customizer shown here.

docs.title: Reactive MongoDB Panache with Kotlin coroutines

docker compose up -d mongodb

Then start the application from the mongodb-kotlin-co directory:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

docs.title: Receive and send multipart data
docs.text: The multipart module demonstrates multipart form input and multipart output with Quarkus REST. The two workflows below distinguish receiving a multipart request from sending one and returning a multipart response.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
The module uses Java 25 and Quarkus 4.0.0.CR1. Its POM includes quarkus-rest, quarkus-rest-jackson, and the REST client extensions. Start the application from the multipart directory:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev.

docs.title: Receive multipart form data
docs.text:
The root POST / resource consumes multipart/form-data into MultipartBody. The form maps the file part to a File, declares its media type as text/csv, and also accepts test, checked, and choice form fields. MultipartResource reads these values from the body object.

The alternative POST /upload2 method accepts MultipartFormDataInput; it demonstrates the low-level input type, but the sample method currently returns ok without reading individual parts.

The MultipartResourceTest sends a request with those fields and the module's test.csv file. From the multipart directory, run the focused test:

./mvnw test

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd test.

docs.title: Send multipart form data and return multipart output
docs.text:
The test demonstrates sending a multipart request with REST Assured. Its file part is named file and uses the text/csv media type:

given()
    .formParam("test", "a String field")
    .formParam("checked", "true")
    .formParam("choice", "YES")
    .multiPart("file", new File("test.csv"), "text/csv")
    .when().post("")
    .then()
    .statusCode(200);

You can send the same form from the multipart module directory with curl:

curl.exe -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/ `
  -F "file=@test.csv;type=text/csv" `
  -F "test=a String field" `
  -F "checked=true" `
  -F "choice=YES"

The sample resource responds with ok. The test.csv file is in the multipart project directory.

The resource also demonstrates a multipart response. GET /output returns a MultipartFormDataOutput with a JSON user part and an XML user part. Send a GET request to http://localhost:8080/output to inspect its response:

curl.exe -i http://localhost:8080/output

The module's Jackson customizer omits empty values and serializes date-time values without timestamps. See Customize Jackson.

docs.title: Document a REST API with OpenAPI and Swagger UI
docs.text: The rest-classic module combines RESTEasy Classic with the quarkus-smallrye-openapi extension. Its PostResources uses MicroProfile OpenAPI annotations such as @Operation, @Parameter, @RequestBody, and @APIResponse to describe endpoint behavior, inputs, schemas, and response headers.

docs.title: Generated endpoints
docs.text:
When the rest-classic application is running in development mode, the generated OpenAPI document is available at:

  • http://localhost:8080/q/openapi for YAML.
  • http://localhost:8080/q/openapi?format=json for JSON.
  • http://localhost:8080/q/swagger-ui for Swagger UI.

Swagger UI is available by default in development and test modes. The generated document includes JAX-RS endpoints and uses explicit OpenAPI annotations where the sample provides them. For example, the create-post operation documents its request body, 201 response, and Location header.

docs.title: Run and inspect the sample
docs.text:
From the rest-classic directory, start development mode:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev. Open http://localhost:8080/q/swagger-ui or request the OpenAPI document with curl.exe http://localhost:8080/q/openapi.

The module already includes quarkus-smallrye-openapi in its POM. Its application.properties contains commented examples for changing the OpenAPI and Swagger UI paths. They are comments, so the default paths above are currently in effect.

docs.title: Include Swagger UI in production
docs.text:
Swagger UI is normally limited to development and test. To include it in a production build, add this build-time setting to the module's application.properties:

quarkus.swagger-ui.always-include=true

Only enable this when the UI is intended to be publicly available; the OpenAPI document and interactive UI can expose API structure to users.

docs.title: Reactive PostgreSQL Client
docs.text: The rest-pgclient module accesses PostgreSQL with the reactive SQL client and Mutiny. It maps rows to Java records directly instead of using an ORM.

docs.title: Java HTTP Client
docs.text: The restclient-classic-java11 module uses the JDK's java.net.http.HttpClient to call the posts service. It sends asynchronous requests and maps response bodies with JSON-B.

docs.title: Inspect the client
docs.text:
PostResourceClient builds an HTTP/2 client and calls the service with sendAsync. It parses count responses as text and converts JSON response bodies to Java objects with an injected Jsonb instance. The module includes RESTEasy Classic and JSON-B, but the outbound calls use the JDK HTTP client.

The sample currently uses http://localhost:8080 in its request URIs. The application.properties sets the local Quarkus HTTP port to 8081.

docs.title: JAX-RS Client API
docs.text: The restclient-classic-jaxrs module creates an outbound client with ClientBuilder. It uses the JAX-RS Client API directly rather than registering a MicroProfile REST Client interface.

docs.title: Configure and call the service
docs.text:
PostResourceClient reads its baseUrl from PostServiceProperties, which maps post-service.base_url. The module's application.properties sets that value to http://localhost:8080 and listens locally on port 8081.

The client uses ClientBuilder, query parameters, typed entity reads, and asynchronous JAX-RS invocations that return CompletionStage. The POM includes the RESTEasy Classic Client and Jackson client extensions. See Jackson on REST clients.

The client also exposes an SSE endpoint through SseEventSource, registering SseEventProvider on the Client so text/event-stream responses can be read.

docs.title: Mock the service in tests
docs.text:
WireMockTestResource implements QuarkusTestResourceLifecycleManager: it starts a WireMockServer on a dynamic port and returns that URL for the post-service.base_url key named by a @ResourceArg on @QuarkusTestResource. The test injects the server with @InjectWireMock and calls stubFor, verify, and resetAll on that instance rather than the static DSL, because the DSL's default client is thread-local and would keep pointing at port 8080.

The SSE test is @Disabled. WireMock buffers the whole response body, so a simulated text/event-stream never reaches end-of-stream and SseEventSource fires neither its event nor its completion consumer; chunkedDribbleDelay and a Connection: close header were both tried. See Mock HTTP peers.

docs.title: Run the client
docs.text:
Start a posts service at the configured base URL, then run the client from restclient-classic-jaxrs:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev.

docs.title: MicroProfile REST Client with RESTEasy Classic
docs.text: The restclient-classic module declares its posts client as a JAX-RS interface and runs the client with RESTEasy Classic. Its methods return CompletionStage values.

docs.title: Declare the client
docs.text:
PostResourceClient uses @RegisterRestClient(configKey = "post-service") and @RegisterProvider for its response exception mapper. It exposes count, list, and by-ID operations. Its POM includes quarkus-resteasy-client and quarkus-resteasy-client-jsonb.

The module configures the client URL and listens on port 8081:

quarkus.http.port=8081
quarkus.rest-client.post-service.url=http://localhost:8080
quarkus.rest-client.post-service.scope=jakarta.inject.Singleton

The JSON-B client provider is supplied by the module's quarkus-resteasy-client-jsonb extension. See JSON-B on REST clients.

docs.text:
Start the posts service on port 8080, then run the client from restclient-classic:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev. The client application uses port 8081.

The module sets port 8081 and points the client at http://localhost:8080 through the configKey declared on @RegisterRestClient:

quarkus.http.port=8081
quarkus.rest-client.post-service.url=http://localhost:8080
quarkus.rest-client.post-service.scope=jakarta.inject.Singleton

A simple configKey is required for testing: the Quarkiverse WireMock dev service repoints quarkus.rest-client.<configKey>.url when the test class is annotated with @ConnectWireMock(restClient = "post-service"). See Mock HTTP peers.

docs.title: Build a GraphQL API with SmallRye GraphQL
docs.text: The graphql module exposes a GraphQL API with SmallRye GraphQL. It demonstrates queries, a mutation, a computed field, and a subscription. Its posts store is in memory and does not persist data to a database.

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
From the graphql directory, run:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev. The GraphQL endpoint is http://localhost:8080/graphql.

docs.title: Inspect the API
docs.text:
The module uses quarkus-smallrye-graphql. Its GraphQLResource declares:

  • allPosts and postById queries.
  • A createPost mutation.
  • A countOfComments field resolver that reads the source Post.
  • A postCreated subscription that returns a Mutiny Multi.

The PostService stores posts in an in-memory list and publishes creation events through a broadcast processor.

docs.title: Validate inputs and handle errors
docs.text: createPost accepts a @Valid CreatePost input, so the input object's Jakarta Bean Validation constraints are applied to mutations. The sample defines PostNotFoundException with the SmallRye @ErrorCode annotation and configures GraphQL error extension fields in application.properties. This demonstrates returning a machine-readable error code and exposing selected error details; review the sample's settings before exposing exception messages in a public API.

docs.title: Send a query
docs.text:
Send a GraphQL request to the endpoint. In PowerShell, run:

curl.exe -X POST http://localhost:8080/graphql `
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" `
  --data-raw '{"query":"{ allPosts { id title content countOfComments } }"}'

The response contains the selected fields under data.allPosts.

docs.title: Exercise the server from a test
docs.text: The module ships a @QuarkusTest (GraphQLResourceDynamicClientTest) that calls the running application through SmallRye's dynamic client API (DynamicGraphQLClient, added in test scope via quarkus-smallrye-graphql-client). Injecting the client with an empty @GraphQLClient("") config key makes Quarkus point it at the application's own /graphql endpoint automatically, so no url has to be configured. The test asserts on real results: the seeded allPosts, a postById lookup passed as a postId argument, and a createPost mutation whose input is sent as a CreatePostInput variable.

docs.title: Typesafe SmallRye GraphQL client
docs.text: The graphql-client module declares a typesafe GraphQL API with @GraphQLClientApi. Use this client when you want GraphQL operations and response types represented as Java methods.

docs.title: Configure the client
docs.text:
The PostGraphQLClient uses config key post-client-typesafe. The module points it at http://localhost:8080/graphql:

quarkus.smallrye-graphql-client.post-client-typesafe.url=http://localhost:8080/graphql

The PostGraphQLClient declares list and summary queries, a query that returns ErrorOr<Post>, and a mutation. The client interface uses the GraphQL API types from the graphql-client module.

ErrorOr<Post> is the sample's explicit way to represent a GraphQL operation that may return an error alongside its data. Inspect the result before using the post value; a GraphQL response can contain both data and errors, and an HTTP-success status alone does not mean every requested field succeeded.

docs.title: Run the client
docs.text:
Start the graphql server on port 8080, then run the graphql-client module:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev. The module's Main class calls the typesafe client along with the other client examples.

docs.title: Part 5: Messaging
docs.text:
Each messaging recipe uses one connector or messaging API. Most samples use the same HTTP façade: POST /messages sends a text message, and GET /messages streams received messages as JSON server-sent events. The JMS sample uses Jakarta Messaging directly; the other samples use SmallRye Reactive Messaging.

Choose the recipe that matches the connector and broker you want to explore:

  • Reactive Messaging with AMQP
  • AMQP with RabbitMQ
  • Reactive Messaging with RabbitMQ
  • JMS with Qpid JMS
  • Reactive Messaging with Pulsar
  • Reactive Messaging with Kafka

These modules are separate applications with separate broker settings. Do not assume one broker URL or Compose file works for another module.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• See Miscellaneous examples.
  • See REST clients for HTTP integrations.

docs.title: AMQP with RabbitMQ
docs.text: The amqp-rabbitmq module uses the AMQP 1.0 connector to connect to RabbitMQ. It keeps the AMQP connector configuration separate from the RabbitMQ-specific SmallRye connector in the rabbitmq module.

docs.title: Configure the AMQP channels
docs.text:
The module sends to and receives from the messages address:

mp.messaging.outgoing.send.connector=smallrye-amqp
mp.messaging.outgoing.send.address=messages
mp.messaging.outgoing.send.use-anonymous-sender=false
mp.messaging.incoming.messages.connector=smallrye-amqp
mp.messaging.incoming.messages.durable=false

The module's Compose file starts RabbitMQ with the quarkus development account and labels the service for AMQP Dev Services discovery.

docs.title: Start RabbitMQ and the application
docs.text:
From the amqp-rabbitmq directory, start the broker:

docker compose up -d

Then start the Quarkus application in the same directory:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev.

docs.title: Send and receive a message
docs.text: The HTTP façade accepts POST /messages with a plain-text body and exposes GET /messages as a JSON server-sent event stream. MessageHandler sends through the outgoing send channel and transforms incoming strings into timestamped messages.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:

  • See Reactive Messaging with RabbitMQ for its native exchange and queue configuration.

docs.title: Reactive Messaging with AMQP
docs.text: The amqp module connects SmallRye Reactive Messaging channels to an AMQP broker. It sends strings to the messages address, consumes the incoming channel, and streams timestamped messages over HTTP.

docs.title: Configure channels
docs.text:
The module uses smallrye-amqp for both channels:

mp.messaging.outgoing.send.connector=smallrye-amqp
mp.messaging.outgoing.send.address=messages
mp.messaging.incoming.messages.connector=smallrye-amqp
mp.messaging.incoming.messages.durable=true

The module's application.properties also declares the AMQP development credentials. Keep credentials in local configuration rather than copying them into application code.

docs.title: Follow the message flow
docs.text: MessageHandler sends to the send channel with an Emitter<String>. Its @Incoming("messages") method transforms a consumed string into a timestamped Message and emits it to messages-stream. The HTTP resource accepts POST /messages and exposes GET /messages as server-sent events.

docs.title: Run the sample
docs.text:
Use the AMQP broker configuration available in Dev Services or the root Compose file. From the amqp directory, run:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev. Check the application logs and MessageResource to confirm the broker-to-stream flow.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Compare the AMQP transport to RabbitMQ in AMQP with RabbitMQ.
  • See the RabbitMQ-native connector in RabbitMQ.

docs.title: Jakarta Messaging with Qpid JMS
docs.text: The jms module uses Jakarta Messaging (JMS) APIs with Quarkus Qpid JMS. Unlike the other messaging modules, it creates and manages a JMS context, queue, producer, and consumer directly rather than using Reactive Messaging.

docs.title: Configure the JMS connection
docs.text:
The module sets the Qpid JMS URL and username in application.properties. Its local Compose file starts an Artemis broker that listens on port 5672. Review the local broker credentials when configuring your environment.

JmsResources produces a JMSContext from the connection factory and creates the HELLO_QUEUE queue.

docs.title: Send and receive messages
docs.text: MessageProducer serializes timestamped messages with JSON-B and sends them to the JMS queue. MessageConsumer consumes messages asynchronously, deserializes them, and publishes them to a Mutiny stream. The HTTP resource accepts POST /messages and exposes GET /messages as server-sent events.

docs.title: Start Artemis and the application
docs.text:
From the jms directory, start Artemis:

docker compose up -d

Then run the application:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev.

docs.text:
• Compare Reactive Messaging channels in AMQP.
  • See Pulsar and Kafka for their connectors.

docs.title: Reactive Messaging with Kafka
docs.text: The kafka module uses SmallRye Reactive Messaging with Kafka. The outgoing channel is named send; the incoming messages channel consumes from the same-named Kafka topic.

docs.title: Configure the Kafka channels
docs.text:
The module's settings include:

%prod.kafka.bootstrap.servers=kafka:9092
mp.messaging.outgoing.send.connector=smallrye-kafka
mp.messaging.incoming.messages.connector=smallrye-kafka
mp.messaging.incoming.messages.topic=send
mp.messaging.incoming.messages.group.id=${quarkus.uuid}

The sample enables earliest offset reset and automatic topic creation. The bootstrap server override is active in the prod profile. Check the development configuration and broker setup for the profile you run.

docs.title: Follow the message flow
docs.text: The HTTP resource sends plain text to the outgoing send channel. The messages channel consumes the send topic, and the handler publishes timestamped messages to messages-stream. GET /messages exposes the stream as server-sent events.

docs.title: Run the sample
docs.text:
From the kafka directory, run:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev. The POM and Quarkus Dev Services configuration provide the broker setup options; choose the provider in the module configuration if needed.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Compare Pulsar.
  • See AMQP with RabbitMQ.

docs.title: Reactive Messaging with Pulsar
docs.text: The pulsar module connects SmallRye Reactive Messaging channels to Apache Pulsar. Its outgoing channel publishes to the messages topic; the incoming channel consumes from Pulsar.

docs.title: Configure the topic
docs.text:
The sample uses these channel settings:

%prod.pulsar.client.serviceUrl=pulsar://pulsar:6650
mp.messaging.outgoing.send.connector=smallrye-pulsar
mp.messaging.outgoing.send.topic=messages
mp.messaging.incoming.messages.connector=smallrye-pulsar
mp.messaging.incoming.messages.subscriptionInitialPosition=Earliest

The Pulsar service URL is set for the prod profile. Configure the broker host and service URL appropriate to your environment before using another profile.

docs.title: Send and stream a message
docs.text: The HTTP façade accepts a text message at POST /messages. The outgoing send channel publishes it to Pulsar. The incoming messages channel transforms consumed text into a timestamped message, which GET /messages streams as JSON server-sent events.

docs.title: Run the sample
docs.text:
Start a Pulsar broker reachable at the configured service URL. Then run the application from the pulsar directory:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:

  • See AMQP for an AMQP broker connector.

docs.title: Reactive Messaging with RabbitMQ
docs.text: The rabbitmq module uses the SmallRye Reactive Messaging RabbitMQ connector. It configures a named exchange and queue rather than using the AMQP 1.0 connector.

docs.title: Configure the exchange and queue
docs.text:
The outgoing channel publishes to the messages exchange. The incoming channel reads from the messages queue and exchange:

mp.messaging.outgoing.send.connector=smallrye-rabbitmq
mp.messaging.outgoing.send.exchange.name=messages
mp.messaging.incoming.messages.connector=smallrye-rabbitmq
mp.messaging.incoming.messages.queue.name=messages
mp.messaging.incoming.messages.exchange.name=messages

The module's configuration references RabbitMQ Dev Services. Its host and credentials are commented examples, so check the local broker configuration before starting the application.

docs.title: Run the sample
docs.text:
Start a RabbitMQ broker using Dev Services or your local environment. From the rabbitmq directory, run:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev.

The HTTP interface accepts POST /messages and streams received messages from GET /messages as server-sent events.

docs.text:

  • See Kafka for a partitioned log connector.

docs.title: Browse legacy samples
docs.text:
The repository's legacy directory preserves earlier examples that use Java 8, RxJava 2, and older Vert.x or Hibernate Reactive APIs. Use these projects for historical comparison; use the modules listed in the other cookbook parts for current sample patterns.

The preserved projects are java8, rxjava2, vertx-routes-java8, hibernate-reactive-java8, and restclient-mutiny. Their source and build files are the reference for their original dependencies and runtime requirements. The reactive walkthrough in the original article archive also discusses historical CompletionStage and RxJava approaches; those are not presented as current recipes.

docs.title: Use the Quarkus CLI
docs.text: Use the Quarkus CLI to run and build a Quarkus project from its module directory, or to add an extension. This recipe uses the repository's rest module as an example; it does not cover every CLI command.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text: Install the Quarkus CLI and Java. See the Quarkus CLI installation guide for platform-specific setup.

docs.title: Run a sample in development mode
docs.text:
From the repository root, change to the rest module:

cd rest

Start development mode:

quarkus dev

The sample starts on port 8080. Its PostgreSQL Dev Services configuration requires a working container runtime. Stop the process with Ctrl+C.

docs.title: Build the sample
docs.text:
From the rest module, create a build:

quarkus build

The CLI detects the project's build tool and delegates to it. Check the build output for errors before running the packaged application.

docs.title: Add an extension
docs.text:
To add an extension to a Quarkus project, run the command from that project's directory. For example, to add SmallRye OpenAPI:

quarkus extension add quarkus-smallrye-openapi

This updates the project dependencies. The repository's rest-classic sample already includes SmallRye OpenAPI, so you do not need to add it there. See OpenAPI and Swagger UI for that sample.

For more CLI commands, see the Quarkus CLI guide.

docs.title: Use the Quarkus Maven plugin
docs.text: The Quarkus Maven plugin integrates Quarkus tasks with Maven. This recipe shows how to run development mode, package a sample, and add an extension with the wrapper in the rest module.

docs.title: Run development mode
docs.text:
From the repository root, change to the rest module:

cd rest

Start the application in development mode:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev. The sample starts on port 8080 and uses PostgreSQL Dev Services, which requires a working container runtime. Stop the process with Ctrl+C.

docs.title: Package the application
docs.text:
From the rest module, run Maven's package lifecycle:

./mvnw clean package

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd clean package. This runs the configured Maven lifecycle, including the Quarkus build. Check the command output for build or test failures.

docs.title: Add an extension
docs.text:
The original getting-started article demonstrates adding JSON-B, validation, OpenAPI, persistence, and JDBC extensions through the Maven plugin. To add an extension to a project, run the command from that project's directory:

./mvnw quarkus:add-extension -Dextensions=quarkus-smallrye-openapi

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:add-extension -Dextensions=quarkus-smallrye-openapi. This updates the project's dependencies. The repository's rest-classic module already has the OpenAPI extension; see OpenAPI and Swagger UI for its configuration and endpoints.

The archived original getting-started article uses early Quarkus plugin versions and syntax. Use the commands on this page for current sample workflows, and check the Quarkus Maven plugin guide for other goals.

docs.title: Schedule tasks with Quartz
docs.text: The quartz module demonstrates persistent Quartz scheduling with a JDBC job store, Hibernate ORM, Flyway, and PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Inspect the sample
docs.text:
The module's application.properties configures quarkus.quartz.store-type as jdbc_cmt, disables clustering, and enables Flyway migration at startup. The production profile configures PostgreSQL at localhost with the quarkus_test database. Hibernate schema generation is disabled.

TaskResource exposes the task HTTP API, and TaskBean implements the scheduled work. Review the module's Flyway migrations and Compose file before using a local database.

docs.title: Run the sample
docs.text:
Start PostgreSQL according to the module's Compose and application configuration. From the quartz directory, run:

./mvnw quarkus:dev

On Windows, run mvnw.cmd quarkus:dev. Run ./mvnw test to execute tests.
